one_liner: Single-header C++11 typed CSV reader; beats vincentlaucsb/csv-parser on single-worker raw reads of files around 30 MB.
what_it_does: Reads CSV/TSV files into a fixed, compile-time number of typed columns: you declare io::CSVReader<N, policies...>, call read_header with the column names you want (it reorders columns by header and can ignore extras), then loop on read_row(a, b, c...) which fills ints, floats, char, std::string or a zero-copy char* into the buffer. It is a different interface from csv-parser's dynamic CSVRow model, not a drop-in. A lower-level LineReader returns one null-terminated line at a time from a file, FILE*, istream, memory range or a custom ByteSourceBase.
how_it_is_fast: Input is read unbuffered (setvbuf _IONBF) in 1 MiB blocks into a 3 MiB buffer, and a background std::thread prefetches the next block while the caller parses the current one (double buffering that overlaps disk I/O with parsing). Lines and fields are tokenized in place by writing NUL terminators into the buffer, so char* columns cost no copy or allocation. Trimming, quoting, overflow and comment handling are template policy classes resolved at compile time, so disabled features add no branches. There is no SIMD: separators and newlines are found with plain byte loops (about 315-350 MB/s in the cited run, derived from the result JSON).
when_to_use: Fixed-schema files (known column names and types) where you want typed values straight into local variables with a tiny loop.
Large single-line-per-record files read sequentially on one core, where a 1 MiB block prefetch thread helps hide disk latency.
Projects that need a vendorable single header with no dependencies and a C++11 floor.
Pipelines that read char* columns and do their own parsing (std::from_chars etc.) to stay zero-copy.
Simple TSV or custom-separator files where quoting can be compiled out entirely for extra speed.
when_not_to_use: Any file that may contain quoted fields with embedded line breaks: these are unsupported and throw escaped_string_not_closed (README FAQ, open issue #92).
Variable or unknown column counts, or schemas only known at runtime: column count is a template parameter (open issues #140, #119).
Numeric data where exact double round-tripping matters: the built-in float parser is not correctly rounded (open issue #122).
Multi-core throughput on large files: csv-parser's 4-8 worker speculative mode and its mmap count path beat it at 5M rows, and SIMD parsers such as zsv go much faster.
Projects wanting an actively maintained library: last commit 2025-02-02, 21 open issues, no tagged release (issue #99).

integration.dependencies: none beyond the C++ standard library; uses std::thread, so GCC builds need -lpthread unless CSV_IO_NO_THREAD is defined
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (README; developed with GCC 4.6.1). Open issue #77 reports a build failure with VS 2017 in C++17 mode; the 2026 comparison builds it with MSVC 19.50 in C++20.
integration.platforms: any platform with a C++11 compiler; no SIMD or architecture-specific code; handles \n and \r\n line endings and skips a UTF-8 BOM
integration.thread_safety: Not documented beyond: each reader owns one background I/O thread (started only when the input exceeds 2 MiB), and a custom ByteSourceBase::read may be called from either thread but never concurrently. Treat each reader as single-consumer; separate readers share no globals in csv.h.

gotchas: Float parsing is hand-rolled (digit accumulation plus repeated multiplication for exponents), not correctly rounded: issue #122 (open since 2021) shows 9.855536508 read as 9.8555365080000054 instead of 9.8555365080000001, although the README says the input 'is rounded to the next floating point'. Read char* and use std::from_chars or strtod when exactness matters.
Empty numeric cells parse silently as 0 (the integer and float parsers accept an empty string, and a lone '-' or '.' also yields 0); there is no NaN/inf support.
The current csv.h limits a line to block_len = 2^20 bytes (about 1 MiB) and throws line_length_limit_exceeded, while the README and the exception text still say 2^24-1.

Defaults are not RFC 4180: CSVReader<N> uses no_quote_escape (quoted commas split columns) and trims spaces and tabs; you must opt into double_quote_escape<',','"'>, and quoted fields keep inner spaces because trimming happens before unquoting.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over zsv or DuckDB's CSV reader when you want a dependency-free single header that hands typed values of a known schema to C++ code; pick zsv for SIMD throughput, dynamic columns and multiline quoted fields, and DuckDB when you want SQL or columnar loading rather than a row loop.
verified_claims_summary: In csv-parser's own Windows comparison (MSVC 19.50, C++20 Release, i5-12400, Google Benchmark median of 5 repetitions, warm 8-column files of about 29 MB at 500K rows and 297 MB at 5M rows), fast-cpp-csv-parser read 500K rows in 81.8-136.2 ms versus 146.5-223.5 ms for csv-parser (about 1.6-2.0x) and won the 5M clean read (944 ms vs 1,087 ms), but lost the 5M count runs, the 5M quoted read, both materialization tables and the positional-read table once csv-parser used 4 or more parser workers. Its throughput was flat at about 315-350 MB/s across sizes, whereas csv-parser's count path rose from about 196 MB/s at 500K to 543 MB/s at 5M (derived from the result JSON), so the 500K wins mostly reflect csv-parser's fixed per-reader start-up cost rather than a faster parsing loop.
status_note: Stale (last commit 2025-02-02, open bugs on float precision and multiline fields unanswered) but BSD-3-Clause, a single 1,200-line header and easy to vendor; the cited numbers come from the competing project's harness, which copies all 8 fields into std::string for fast-cpp while csv-parser takes string_views, and which compiles csv-parser's binaries with /arch:AVX2 (a PUBLIC option on the csv target) while the standalone fast-cpp binary that produced the raw-throughput table gets no AVX2 flag.
